title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Judicial Processes: A Socio-Technical Scoping Review of Architectures, Tasks, and Institutional Risks (2023–Mid-2026)
content: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in legal research, litigation support, and judicial administration. This scoping review maps architectures, court-facing tasks, evaluation designs, and institutional risks in research on GenAI and large language models (LLMs). Framed by Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported with PRISMA-ScR, it screened 1,518 Scopus and Web of Science records (31 March 2026) and 1,000 supplementary Elicit results (July 2026) for publications from 2023 onward, which yielded 201 references. We then reassessed each reference against explicit GenAI and judicial relevance criteria in an AI-assisted workflow checked by one author, with a second screening by a different LLM, and recorded the decisions and reasons. We charted publication characteristics and primary evidence designs and checked selected outcomes against the original publications. The synthesis includes 189 publications. We retained 10 references for context and excluded 2. Offline model evaluations accounted for 106 publications (56.1%). Studies reported task-specific results for retrieval, summarization, prediction, and drafting. One audit of three commercial legal research tools found hallucinations in 17–33% of evaluated queries. The mapped evidence is consistent with source-grounded, reviewable assistance for defined tasks. Heterogeneous evaluations and limited evidence from operating courts constrain conclusions about routine judicial use.
